messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David was 54 when the assault happened, three years before he finally sat in a therapist’s office. He had been working as a private tutor for over a decade, mostly meeting high school and college students in libraries or their homes. One of his regulars was a man in his twenties, someone David had tutored for months without incident. Then one evening, after a session that ran late, the man cornered him in the study, pressed him against the wall, and forced his hands onto David’s body while demanding that David return the touch. David froze—his body would not move, would not shout. Later, he could describe only fragments: the weight of the man’s chest, the carpet against his cheek, the sound of his own breathing. The rest was a cavern of missing seconds. For weeks he could not find words to explain what had happened, even to himself. He told no one.

In the months that followed, David began to notice that physical touch—a student’s accidental brush on the arm, a handshake from a colleague—sent a jolt through him that felt like the start of the assault. The trigger would yank the memory back whole, vivid and sharp, and at the same time it would flood him with the conviction that his body could not be trusted, that it had failed him once and might fail again. That feeling of body unreliability made him even more watchful: he started scanning rooms for anyone who might stand too close, especially men. He became certain that he had to be constantly careful because danger could erupt from anywhere. The more he believed that, the more he avoided unfamiliar places—new coffee shops, the library annex—where he could not assess the exits or the people. At the same time, the memory itself, when it surfaced unbidden, would reignite the same threat monitoring, making him tighten his shoulders and search for the nearest door. He began always choosing a seat with his back to the wall, preferably near an exit, and he watched other people for signs of threat so closely that his eyes ached by the end of a tutoring session.

His negative appraisals—the isolation he felt, the sense that he was set apart from others because no one could understand—also drove his maladaptive strategies. Believing that his body was unreliable and that he had to be on constant guard made him avoid any situation likely to stir strong emotions, because he was afraid of losing control. He also avoided all forms of physical contact, turning down hugs from friends, stepping away when someone reached toward him. And he started smoking more—half a pack a day, then a full pack—because the ritual of lighting up gave him something to do with his hands when anxiety spiked, and the numbness felt like a small shield. The link worked the other way too: whenever a memory of the assault intruded—vivid, detail-laden, yet still fragmented—it strengthened his belief that he was fundamentally separate from other people, that his body had marked him as different. That same memory could also act as a trigger itself, making him feel a ghost of the forced touch, which then escalated his vigilance and sent him reaching for a cigarette.

Now, at fifty-seven, David’s world has narrowed almost entirely. He still tutors, but only female students, and he meets them in public libraries where he can scan the room before choosing a seat. Last month a male student accidentally brushed his shoulder, and David flinched so violently that the student asked if he was okay. David said nothing, but the moment replayed for days. What finally brought him to seek help was not the flinch itself but the loneliness: he realized he had not let anyone hug him in three years, and that the constant wariness was exhausting him. He is most afraid that talking about it will make the memories sharper, but underneath that he is equally afraid that he will never feel safe again—that his own vigilance has become the thing he cannot escape.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., body unreliability) cause or lead to intrusive memories of the assault.
No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., being set apart) cause or increase triggers (e.g., physical touch).
No paragraph conveys that the patient's sense of threat (e.g., feeling of danger) causes or leads to intrusive memories of the assault.
